copy.headline: Trump says Ukraine needs a new president

extended.text: Donald Trump said on Saturday that it is time for Ukraine to get a new president, one 'who can get a deal done' to end the war with Russia. Volodymyr Zelensky, Ukraine's president, 'could have made a lot of deals, but for some reason he never does', Trump told reporters.

The remarks came a day after Trump announced a deal with Vladimir Putin, Russia's president, to import millions of tonnes of Russian diesel. Zelensky called the deal 'a gift to Putin' that gives Russia more money for the war.
Trump said Zelensky has to 'damn well' stop attacking Russian oil and gas plants, which Trump blames for higher fuel prices.

Kirill Dmitriev, a close adviser to Putin, called Trump's statement 'iconic and historic'. Andrii Sybiha, Ukraine's foreign minister, wrote on X that Zelensky 'has the support of the Ukrainian people, and they have the right to decide'. Lars Løkke Rasmussen, Denmark's foreign minister, is among the European politicians backing Zelensky.
On Saturday a Russian attack killed 21 people, four of them children, in Zaporizhzhia, a city in south-eastern Ukraine.

copy.headline: Ireland proposes trimming the EU's draft budget by 8 per cent

standard.text: Ireland, which holds the EU presidency, proposed on Saturday to cut the European Commission's draft budget for 2028 to 2034 by 8 per cent, to 1,622 billion euros at constant prices. That is still about 30 per cent more than the current budget.

Farming, fisheries and regional aid lose only 3 per cent; competitiveness, prosperity and security lose 13. Germany, Denmark, the Netherlands and Sweden, which want money moved from farming towards defence and competitiveness, had sought cuts of 'several hundred billion euros'.
'Still far from an agreement,' said Friedrich Merz, Germany's chancellor. EU leaders take up the proposal at a summit in Brussels next week.

copy.headline: Denmark reminds 1,039 firms of security rules after a leak of 8.8 million ID numbers

standard.text: The CPR administration, which runs Denmark's register of personal identity numbers, wrote on Friday to the 1,039 companies with access to the register, among them financial firms, telecoms companies and law firms. Each must have a security officer, check staff access and track its monthly lookups for misuse.

Using a former employee's leaked password, a hacker had access to the register through Pays, an IT company on Funen, for 21 days and 17 hours; outsiders gained access to 8.8 million ID numbers. Politiken found that at least three Pays profiles, the administrator's among them, used the password '123456'.
Christina Egelund, the digitalisation minister, admits security was not good enough.

short.text: The CPR administration, which runs Denmark's register of personal identity numbers, wrote on Friday to the 1,039 companies with access to the register to remind them of its security rules. Outsiders had gained access to 8.8 million ID numbers through Pays, an IT company on Funen.

copy.headline: Denmark's foreign minister says Trump's diesel deal must not undermine sanctions on Russia

standard.text: Lars Løkke Rasmussen, the foreign minister, said on Saturday that the EU's work on sanctions against Russia 'must not be undermined' by a diesel deal between Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin. Extra income for Russia could in the end pay for the war in Ukraine, he told DR.

Under the deal, Trump says, Russia will at once deliver 300,000 tonnes of diesel to the American and global market. The US Treasury has given temporary permission for sanctions to be eased so that Russia can sell diesel internationally, until 7 April 2027 according to Reuters.
Volodymyr Zelensky, Ukraine's president, wrote on Friday that the deal would give Russia more money to wage war.

short.text: Lars Løkke Rasmussen, the foreign minister, said on Saturday that the EU's work on sanctions against Russia 'must not be undermined' by Donald Trump's diesel deal with Vladimir Putin, which America has backed by temporarily easing sanctions on Russian diesel.

copy.deck: America has temporarily eased sanctions to let Russia sell diesel; Ukraine's president says the deal gives Moscow more money for war.

copy.headline: Denmark's crown prince says he is open to deployment

standard.text: Crown Prince Christian, heir to the Danish throne, is open to staying in the military after he qualifies as a lieutenant, and would 'definitely find it interesting' to be deployed, he told Politiken. He did not say where.
He became a second lieutenant this summer and is now a platoon leader in the Royal Life Guards, an infantry regiment of the Danish army, helping to train conscripts.

He doubted his choice when he began conscription in February 2025: 'On the drive down there I was shaking all over,' he said. In the interview he also spoke for the first time about press interest in videos of him at a music festival this summer.
